markup: She'd never stolen anything. Not even a paperclip.
Then she read one sign...
and wanted to steal.
Arizona's Petrified Forest.
Visitors kept pocketing little pieces.
So the park put up a warning:
It said... "Warning!
{14|Fourteen} tons stolen every year... one small piece at a time."
She read it, leaned over to her {fiancé,|fee-ahn-say,} and whispered:
"We'd better get ours now."
But why would a warning make an honest person want to steal?
Her {fiancé's|fee-ahn-say's} professor, psychologist Robert {Cialdini,|Chal-dee-nee,} tested it.
His team hid marked wood along the trails, and kept swapping the signs.
One sign said: "Please don't take the wood."
The other said: "Many visitors take the wood."
With "please don't," only {2%|two percent} of the pieces vanished.
With "many visitors"...
almost {8%.|eight percent.}
You see, we don't copy rules.
We copy each other.
"Many people steal" doesn't sound like a warning.
It sounds like what everyone does.
Like a teacher saying, "Half this class cheated."
The other half hears: everybody cheats.
The sign didn't stop thieves.
It gave them permission.
And the bait wood?
It came from the park's "conscience pile":
pieces people stole, then mailed back with apology letters.
So some of it got stolen twice.
